headline: Peconic settles into high summer — porgies deep and steady, bass gone nocturnal
subhead: The bay's warmed past the point where stripers want daylight, but porgies, fluke, and weakfish are keeping rods bent from Shelter Island to Sag Harbor.
body_markdown:
By the first week of August the Peconic has settled into that thick, warm rhythm it gets every summer once the surface climbs into the mid-to-upper 70s. This bay always runs a few degrees ahead of the Sound and the ocean beaches, and that head start cuts both ways this time of year — it got the bass biting weeks before everyone else back in April, and now it's pushing them into the same deep, nocturnal pattern the rest of the coast is only just starting to see. I've fished this water long enough to expect it. Doesn't mean I like it, but I know how to work around it.

We flagged this last week — said the pattern here would stay quiet and stable with no real disruption on the horizon — and that's exactly how it's played out. No fronts, no big temperature swings, just steady warm water and a bite that rewards anglers willing to fish the right structure at the right stage of the tide rather than expecting a blitz to show up on its own.

Stripers are still around, but they've pushed off the flats and into deeper holes and channel edges, feeding mostly after dark or in that gray window right at first light. Robins Island's west side, the drop-off outside Jessup Neck, and the deeper bend of Noyack Bay have all given up fish in the 26 to 34-inch range to guys drifting live eels or bunker chunks on the bottom during the last two hours of the outgoing. If you're set on daytime bass, your best shot is working the current seams around the Shelter Island ferry docks or the rips off Cedar Island Point where the moving water keeps things cooler and the bait stacks up. Bucktails in the 1 to 1.5-ounce range, white or chartreuse, worked slow along bottom on the down-current side, have taken a few keeper-class fish for me this week — not a pile, but enough to make the stops worthwhile.

Porgies are the story right now, and they haven't slowed a step. The deeper holes around Shelter Island — the classic spots off Hay Beach, the drop just outside Coecles Harbor, and the flats-to-channel transition near Big Ram Island — are holding thick schools in 18 to 25 feet of water. Standard hi-lo rigs with size 4 or 6 hooks, tipped with squid strips or sandworms, are producing steady doubles on the last two hours of the incoming and first hour of the outgoing, when the current's still got some push but isn't ripping. These aren't just the usual 9 and 10-inch pan-sized fish either — I've had several better than 12 inches over the rail this week, which tells me there's a good class of porgies moving through ahead of what should be an excellent fall run.

Fluke fishing has stayed exactly what it's been most of the summer — dependable, not spectacular. The channels running between Nassau Point and Robins Island, along with the deeper cuts off Southold and the mouth of Sag Harbor Cove, are holding keepers mixed with plenty of shorts on drifts through 15 to 25 feet. White or pink Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow with the drift rather than worked hard, have been out-fishing bait rigs for me the last two weeks. The bite's better on the moving stages of the tide — either direction — and dead slack tends to shut it down completely, so plan your drifts around the push rather than fighting through the lulls.

Weakfish are still showing in modest numbers, mostly at dusk and into the early dark around the deeper holes in Three Mile Harbor and the flats off Northwest Creek. Nothing to build a whole trip around, but if you're already out there for bass at last light, a bucktail tipped with a strip of squid worked slow along bottom has picked up a few nice ones in the 4 to 6-pound class. Bluefish, meanwhile, are enjoying this warm stretch as much as anything in the bay — good numbers of choppers in the 3 to 6-pound range are running the surface around Orient Point and along the edges of the main channel, especially on bunker pods that have been thick this week. Wire leaders or heavy fluorocarbon are a must if you're throwing poppers or metal at them, because they'll bite through anything lighter without slowing down.

Looking ahead, I don't see much reason for this pattern to break in the next several days. Water's stable, tides are building slightly as we work toward the next new moon, and that added current strength should sharpen up the porgy and fluke bites on the stronger stages of the tide even more. If a cold front or heavy rain moves through and knocks the surface temperature down even a couple degrees, watch for the stripers to shift back toward a daytime pattern — that's when I'd expect the flats around Shelter Island and Robins Island to come back alive during normal daylight hours. Until then, fish the moving water, fish the depth, and don't expect the bass to cooperate until the sun goes down. There's also quiet talk starting up at the docks about bay scallop season prep — a little early yet, but it's a sure sign everyone around here already has one eye on fall.
